analysis.one_liner: Bans manufacture, import, and sale of firefighting foam containing PFAS 'forever chemicals'.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, where it died without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal under the Toxic Substances Control Act to make, import, process, or sell any aqueous film-forming firefighting foam containing PFAS, a class of long-lasting 'forever chemicals' linked to cancer and other health harms [S2][S3]. Foam with PFAS has been standard equipment for decades, and firefighters are exposed to it repeatedly in training and emergencies [S2]. It would also require the EPA to ban fluorinated chemicals in firefighting foam at all airports by October 2024 [S2][S3]. The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate committee to which it was referred [S1][S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Firefighters, who face elevated cancer risk from repeated exposure to PFAS foam, and communities whose drinking water is contaminated by foam runoff near airports, military bases, and fire training sites [S2].

how_it_helps.text: It bans the manufacture, import, processing, and sale of firefighting foam containing PFAS, removing a direct route of exposure for firefighters who use it in training and emergencies [S2][S3].
It requires a ban on fluorinated chemicals in firefighting foam at airports by October 2024, building on a transition already mandated in the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018 [S2][S3].
Violations would be enforceable under the Toxic Substances Control Act, giving the prohibition legal teeth [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers of fluorinated firefighting foam would lose a market, and airports and fire departments would need to buy fluorine-free alternatives and dispose of existing stock.

drawbacks.text: Airports, fire departments, and other users would have to replace existing foam stock and buy fluorine-free alternatives, which have historically been more expensive and, for some fuel fires, less proven in performance, before fluorine-free foams caught up with the standard the bill requires them to meet [S3].

The bill is narrow: it addresses one product, firefighting foam, and leaves untouched the much larger sources of PFAS contamination, such as industrial discharges and contaminated-site cleanup, which would remain subject to separate regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The health benefit for firefighters and airport-adjacent communities is clear, and the transition costs are real but limited: the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018 had already pushed airports toward fluorine-free foam, so the bill mainly moves an existing transition to a firm deadline rather than creating a wholly new burden [S2][S3]. The main cost falls on the small set of companies that make PFAS-based foam. A fair assessment is that the benefits outweigh the costs, but the bill was too narrow to become the centerpiece of a broader PFAS strategy.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never scheduled a hearing or vote before the two-year Congress ended [S1][S5].

narrative.text: Sen. Gillibrand introduced the bill on April 25, 2022, near the end of the two-year Congress [S1][S5].
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on Environment and Public Works on the day of introduction, and no further action of any kind is recorded [S5].
Only one senator, a Democrat, cosponsored the bill [S4].
The Congress ended January 3, 2023, without the bill receiving a hearing, markup, or floor vote [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers of PFAS-based firefighting foam kept their market, and users of the foam kept the status quo; firefighters gained nothing because the bill died in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PFAS foam makers and the status quo

for.name: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole Senate sponsor; it died in committee.

against.name: Senate Environment and Public Works Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Tom Carper (D-DE)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on the day of introduction and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — before the Congress ended.

against.name: Fluorochemical manufacturers
against.role: Makers of PFAS-based firefighting foam (e.g., 3M, Chemours, Dynéon)
against.what_they_did: The PFAS-fluorochemical industry has opposed and lobbied against restrictions on PFAS products, including foam bans; its interest ran against the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call exists; its only recorded support came from two Democrats (the sponsor and one cosponsor), and no Republican support is recorded [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Fluorochemical manufacturers of PFAS-based firefighting foam
industries.note: The bill would cut off their market for aqueous film-forming foam, a product whose PFAS content exposes firefighters and contaminates groundwater. Its defeat left their revenue stream intact.
Firefighters face elevated cancer risk from repeated PFAS exposure through foam; the ban would remove a direct occupational hazard. The bill's death left that exposure in place.

They would bear transition costs for fluorine-free foam and disposal of old stock, but they also benefit from reduced contamination liability and firefighter safety, and the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2018 had already started the transition the bill would complete.

industries.industry: Makers of fluorine-free firefighting foam alternatives
industries.note: The ban would create a guaranteed market for their products at airports and fire departments.
